Draupadī-ratha
(‘the chariot of द्रौपदी’)
------------------------------------------
There are seven rock-cut temples in Māmallapuram or महाबलिपुरम् near Madras (or Chennai) on the east coast. They are generally called ‘Rathas’ since they resemble a रथ or a chariot in shape. The द्रौपदी-रथ is also one of them. It is the first on the northern side.
It is a simple cell, 3.3 metres (11 ft.) square externally, with a curvilinear roof rising to a height of 5.4 metres (18 ft.). The cell inside measures 1.95 metres in depth by 1.35 metres across (6.5 ft. by 4.5 ft.). On the back wall there is the figure of a female deity (with four arms) and her four attendants. There are also two dvārapālikās (gate-keepers) at the entrance.
It is in Pallava style of architecture and belongs to the 7th cent. A. D.

Draupadī
(‘daughter of Drupada’)
------------------------------------------
Draupadī, also known as Kṛṣṇā (since she was of dark complexion) (kṛṣṇa = dark) and Pāñcālī (since she was the daughter of the king of the country of Pāñcāla) was the chief queen of the five Pāṇḍava princes. She was, in a way, the root-cause of the fratricidal war of कुरु-क्षेत्र.
She was born, along with her brother धृष्टद्युम्न, from the sacrificial fire of Drupada, the king of Pāñcāla. Since she was a damsel of extraordinary beauty, Drupada arranged for her स्वयṁवर (See SVAYAṀVARA.) with very high stakes, in the form of piercing the मत्स्ययन्त्र (See MATSYAYANTRA). अर्जुन succeeded in the feat and was garlanded by her.
When the five Pāṇḍava princes who were then in disguise as forest hermits, announced to their मोथेर् कुन्ती that they had brought an extremely precious alms, कुन्ती who was busy inside the hut, commanded them to ‘share it equally!’ When she actually saw the girl and realised her mistake it was too late! द्रौपदी was then married to all the five brothers. The sage नारद came to the rescue of the brothers stipulating that she should live with each of them for one year by turns and that if any of the others saw her during that period, should go on a पिल्ग्रिमगे for one year as a penance.
In the first गम्ब्लिन्ग् match with the Kauravas, युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, lost his all, including द्रौपदी. Though she was humiliated, she was rescued by the divine intervention of Śrī कृष्ण.
The Pāṇḍavas regained their possessions but युधिष्ठिर lost them again in a second round match. This time they were forced into exile for thirteen years.
After the exile period was over, when the Pāṇḍavas were in a mood to compromise with the Kauravas, द्रौपदी appealed to Śrī कृष्ण to bring about the destruction of the latter through war. Śrī कृष्ण did so. Her anger subsided when दुश्शासन and दुर्योधन were killed in the battle.
When युधिष्ठिर was crowned as the monarch, द्रौपदी became the queen.
During the final journey of the Pāṇḍavas to हेअवेन् (known as ‘mahā-prasthāna’) द्रौपदी was the first to collapse. The reason given by युधिष्ठिर was that she was loving अर्जुन more than the others, though she was expected to love all the five husbands equally.
Draupadī has been considered as an aspect of the मोथेर्-goddess and worshipped as such by the folk-cults of South India. There are numerous shrines dedicated to her in Tamil Nadu and Karna-taka, where an annual ritual festival known as ‘Karaga’ is celebrated. The shrines also contain the icons of धर्म-rāja (or युधिष्ठिर) as her consort.
Iconographically, she is shown as a beautiful lady with three eyes and two arms, the right one holding a lotus. The figure is bent in three places (tribhaṅga).
See also MAHĀBHĀRATA.
